q-125510.name: Question 1
q-125510.problem:
Find the median of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0, \\ \frac{{x}^{3}}{64}, & 0\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & x\ge 4.\end{aligned}
$$
q-125510.worked_solution:
The median of a random variable $X$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
P(X\le m)=F(m)=\frac{{m}^{3}}{64},\,0\le m\le 4.
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\frac{{m}^{3}}{64}=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,m=\sqrt[3]{32}.
$$

q-94598.name: Question 2
q-94598.problem:
Find the median of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}, & 0\le x\le 5, \\ 1, & x>5.\end{aligned}
$$
q-94598.worked_solution:
The median of a random variable $X$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
P(X\le m)=F(m)=\frac{{m}^{2}}{25},\,0\le m\le 5.
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\frac{{m}^{2}}{25}=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,m=\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Note that we took the positive root because $0\le m\le 5.$

q-125516.name: Question 3
q-125516.problem:
Find the median of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0, \\ \frac{x}{3}, & 0\le x\le 2 \\ \frac{{x}^{4}}{195}+\frac{38}{65}, & 2<x\le 3, \\ 1, & x>3.\end{aligned}
$$
q-125516.worked_solution:
The median of a random variable $X$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Since $F(2)=\frac{2}{3}>\frac{1}{2},$ we have $0\le m\le 2.$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\frac{m}{3}=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,m=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

q-125515.name: Question 4
q-125515.problem:
Find the median of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<2, \\ \frac{1}{240}({x}^{4}-16), & 2\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$
q-125515.worked_solution:
The median of a random variable $X$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
P(X\le m)=F(m)=\frac{1}{240}({m}^{4}-16),\,2\le m\le 4.
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\frac{1}{240}({m}^{4}-16)=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,m=\sqrt[4]{136}.
$$

q-94641.name: Question 6
q-94641.problem:
Find the median of the random variable $Y$ if the probability density function of $Y$ is given by

$$
f(y)=\{\begin{aligned}6{e}^{-6y},\, & y\ge 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
q-94641.worked_solution:
The median of a random variable $Y$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(Y\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le m) & ={\int }_{0}^{m}6{e}^{-6y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{e}^{-6y}{|}_{0}^{m} \\  & =1-{e}^{-6m}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-6m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {e}^{-6m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ -6m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\ -6m & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ m & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

q-125714.name: Question 11
q-125714.problem:
Find, to three decimal places, the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}-1}{8}, & 1\le x\le 3, \\ 1, & x>3.\end{aligned}
$$
q-125714.worked_solution:
To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{1}^{2}-1}{8} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {q}_{1}^{2}-1 & =2 \\ {q}_{1}^{2} & =3 \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we take the root ${q}_{1}=\sqrt{3}$ because $1\le {q}_{1}\le 3.$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{3}^{2}-1}{8} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {q}_{3}^{2}-1 & =6 \\ {q}_{3}^{2} & =7 \\ {q}_{3} & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we take the root ${q}_{3}=\sqrt{7}$ because $1\le {q}_{3}\le 3.$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
\begin{aligned}IQR & ={q}_{3}-{q}_{1} \\  & =\sqrt{7}-\sqrt{3} \\  & ≈0.914\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

q-94576.name: Question 12
q-94576.problem:
Find the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<1, \\ 1-{e}^{1-x},\, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$
q-94576.worked_solution:
To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ 1-{e}^{1-{q}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {e}^{1-{q}_{1}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ 1-{q}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) \\ {q}_{1} & =1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ 1-{e}^{1-{q}_{3}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {e}^{1-{q}_{3}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ 1-{q}_{3} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}) \\ {q}_{3} & =1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
\begin{aligned}IQR & ={q}_{3}-{q}_{1} \\  & =1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4})-(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3).\end{aligned}
$$

q-125712.problem:
Find, to three decimal places, the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<0, \\ {x}^{2},\, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 1,\, & x>1.\end{aligned}
$$
q-125712.worked_solution:
To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {q}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {q}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we take the root ${q}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}$ because $0\le {q}_{1}\le 1.$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {q}_{3}^{2} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {q}_{3} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we take the root ${q}_{3}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ because $0\le {q}_{3}\le 1.$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
\begin{aligned}IQR & ={q}_{3}-{q}_{1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2} \\  & ≈0.366\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

q-125522.name: Question 16
q-125522.problem:
Find the $25$th percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{2}-1,\, & 2<x<4, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
q-125522.worked_solution:
The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${x}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {x}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $25$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.25.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.25}) & ={\int }_{2}^{{x}_{0.25}}(\frac{x}{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}-x)|}_{2}^{{x}_{0.25}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.25}^{2}}{4}-{x}_{0.25}-(\frac{(2)^{2}}{4}-2) \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.25}^{2}}{4}-{x}_{0.25}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $25$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{0.25}^{2}}{4}-{x}_{0.25}+1 & =0.25 \\ {x}_{0.25}^{2}-4{x}_{0.25}+3 & =0 \\ ({x}_{0.25}-3)({x}_{0.25}-1) & =0 \\ {x}_{0.25}=1,\,3.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we take the root ${x}_{0.25}=3$ because $2<{x}_{0.25}<4.$

Question 16
?

Find the 25th percentile of the random variable X if the probability distribution function of X is given by f(x)={x2−1,2<x<4,0,otherwise.

a
 3
b
 2−5
c
 1+5
d
 25
e
 1−5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The 100pth percentile of a random variable X is the number xp such that

P(X≤xp)=p.

In our case, we want to find the 25th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal p=0.25. We have

P(X≤x0.25)=∫2x0.25(x2−1)dx=(x24−x)|2x0.25=x0.2524−x0.25−((2)24−2)=x0.2524−x0.25+1.

Therefore, the 25th percentile is given by

x0.2524−x0.25+1=0.25x0.252−4x0.25+3=0(x0.25−3)(x0.25−1)=0x0.25=1,3.

Note that we take the root x0.25=3 because 2<x0.25<4.

q-94701.name: Question 17
q-94701.problem:
Find the $30$th percentile of the random variable $Y$ if the probability distribution function of $Y$ is given by

$$
f(y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-y},\, & y\ge 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
q-94701.worked_solution:
The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $Y$ is the number ${y}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(Y\le {y}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $30$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.3.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le {y}_{0.3}) & ={\int }_{0}^{{y}_{0.3}}{e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{e}^{-y}{|}_{0}^{{y}_{0.3}} \\  & =1-{e}^{-{y}_{0.3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $30$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-{y}_{0.3}} & =0.3 \\ {e}^{-{y}_{0.3}} & =0.7 \\ {e}^{-{y}_{0.3}} & =\frac{7}{10} \\ -{y}_{0.3} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{10}) \\ {y}_{0.3} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{10}{7}) \\ {y}_{0.3} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(7).\end{aligned}
$$

q-94670.problem:
Find the $21$st percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{21}x,\, & 2\le x\le 5, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
q-94670.worked_solution:
The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${x}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {x}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $21$st percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.21.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.21}) & ={\int }_{2}^{{x}_{0.21}}\frac{2}{21}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{21}|}_{2}^{{x}_{0.21}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.21}^{2}}{21}-\frac{4}{21}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $21$st percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{0.21}^{2}}{21}-\frac{4}{21} & =0.21 \\ {x}_{0.21}^{2} & =(0.21)(21)+4 \\ {x}_{0.21} & =2.9.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{x},\, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

q-94705.problem:
Find the $90$th percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}},\, & x\ge 1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
q-94705.worked_solution:
The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${x}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {x}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $90$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.9.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.9}) & ={\int }_{1}^{{x}_{0.9}}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{{x}_{0.9}}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{x}^{-1/2}{|}_{1}^{{x}_{0.9}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}_{0.9}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $90$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}_{0.9}}} & =0.9 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}_{0.9}}} & =0.1 \\ \sqrt{{x}_{0.9}} & =10 \\ {x}_{0.9} & =100.\end{aligned}
$$
